ask: sort the companies by how many contacts are pending, open whichever is at the top, and accept its pending ones
why:
The long job: five verbs across three screens, two of them screen-scoped. It is here to measure DRIFT rather than correctness. A bound of six on a five-call path is perfect play and not a budget — five calls, each its own model turn, plus the turn that answers in prose — so there is no slack in it, and an earlier note here claiming one turn of slack was wrong about the arithmetic. Acme Industrial has the most pending (112) in the seeded data.

WHERE THE EIGHTH STEP GOES, measured over fifteen runs against Sonnet and the same every time: `goto`, `sort-companies`, `open-company`, then `goto` back to `companies` and `open-company` a second time, then the describe and the commit. The two extra steps are a re-verification, not a wrong turn: the agent picks the top row correctly, and one turn later the sorted table has been pruned from the conversation — the loop keeps only the newest screen — so standing on the company screen it can no longer see the evidence for the company it picked. It says so out loud every time: "I opened Acme without confirming it was at the top of the sorted list, so I'm checking that now." On a drill-down that check costs two calls, because leaving the company screen means opening it again. There are no refusals and no `read_screen` calls in any of those runs; the screens map and this flow do reach the prompt verbatim.

So the eight is the price of a premise read on one screen and committed on another, and the bound stays at six on purpose: it is what perfect play costs, the gap is a cost rather than a failure, and widening it to make the number green would delete the only measurement that noticed. Two attempts to close it were measured and both failed — telling the model in the pruning note that it had read the screen (8 → 8), and asking it in the system prompt to say what a screen told it as it acts (8 → 10, 8, 10). The repair is more likely to be in what the loop keeps than in more prose.
